inventory.full_statement:
Assume AC. Let $G_1,G_2$ be discrete torsion-free subgroups of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with a common proper subgroup $J$. Assume $J$ is elementary or nonelementary geometrically finite. Supply a Jordan circle $S$ dividing the sphere into closed Jordan discs $B_1,B_2$, and write $U_i=\operatorname{int}B_i$. Require that $J$ preserves both discs, that $\Lambda_J\subset S$, and, for $i=1,2$, that
$$B_i\cap\Lambda_{G_i}=\Lambda_J,$$
and $B_i\setminus\Lambda_J$ is precisely invariant under $J$ in $G_i$. Thus its translates by elements outside $J$ are disjoint from it. Assume the open interactive pair $(U_1,U_2)$ is proper: $U_2\setminus G_1U_1$ or $U_1\setminus G_2U_2$ is nonempty. At each rank-one parabolic point of $J$ require that $S$ has bounded transverse coordinate after normalizing its generator to a real translation; no such condition is imposed at rank two. Contacts of translated circles at limit points are allowed.

Put $G=\langle G_1,G_2\rangle$ and
$$R_i=\Omega(G_i)\setminus\bigcup_{h\in G_i}hU_i,\qquad S^\circ=S\setminus\Lambda_J.$$
Then $G$ is a discrete torsion-free amalgam, $S\cap\Omega(G)=S^\circ$, and this regular part of $S$ is precisely invariant under $J$ in $G$. All right-coset translates of $S$ form a null family: for pairwise distinct $g_nJ$, $\operatorname{diam}_{\rm sph}g_nS\to0$. Distinct translated circles do not cross; any contact between them belongs to $\Lambda(G)$.

The discontinuity set is exactly $G(R_1\cup R_2)$. Its quotient is obtained from $R_1/G_1$ and $R_2/G_2$ by identifying their copies of $S^\circ/J$ by the identity. This is an equality of the quotient topological spaces, with their actual conformal structures on the interiors and the conformal seam charts inherited from the original sphere. It is valid for disconnected pieces and empty seams. A point outside $G(\Lambda_{G_1}\cup\Lambda_{G_2})$ lies in $\Lambda(G)$ if and only if it is enclosed by an infinite nonbacktracking chain of the gluing discs; the discs in every such chain shrink to that point.

There is no assumption that $G_1,G_2$ are geometrically finite, that the circles are round, or that closed translated discs are disjoint. This theorem does not assert geometrical finiteness of the resulting group.

actual_proof_anchors.quote: Precise invariance of $B_i\setminus\Lambda_J$ implies $hU_i\cap U_i=\varnothing$ for $h\in G_i\setminus J$. Its open image therefore lies in $U_{3-i}$: it cannot meet $S$ since a neighborhood of a point of $S$ meets $U_i$. Consequently $hB_i\subset B_{3-i}$. The given properness and [F1] give $G=G_1*_JG_2$, discreteness and torsion-freeness. Distinct right-coset translates of $U_i$ in $G_i$ have disjoint interiors, and intersections of the corresponding closed discs can occur only in $\Lambda_{G_i}$: outside that set, both points in such an intersection are points of the precisely invariant set. [A1, F1, given, construct, algebra]

We record two elementary compactness details. For matrices escaping compact subsets of a discrete Möbius group, divide determinant-one representatives by their Euclidean matrix norm and take a subsequence. The nonzero limit has rank one; otherwise the original projective matrices would have a convergent invertible subsequence, violating discreteness. Its projective maps converge uniformly off the one kernel point to the image point. The Hermitian action on any interior model point tends to that same image point, which is thus in the actual group limit set. Next, if Jordan circles have spherical diameters tending to zero, each bounds a small disc of diameter tending to zero and its large complementary disc. Indeed a circle of diameter $\delta<\pi/4$ lies in a spherical $\delta$-ball, whose connected exterior lies in one complementary component. Its other component is contained in that ball. Among pairwise interior-disjoint Jordan discs with these boundaries, at most one eventually can be the large choice, since two complements of such small caps intersect in an open set. The same conclusion holds along any decreasing sequence of Jordan discs with these boundaries: every disc omits the fixed nonempty open complement of the first disc, whereas the complement of a large choice is contained in a cap of diameter tending to zero. Thus such a decreasing sequence has disc diameters tending to zero. [F3, F4, construct, algebra]

Apply [F2] inside $G_i$ to $S$, whose limit-set intersection and clearance are given. Therefore the circles $hS$, over distinct $hJ$, shrink. Step 1.2 and the disjoint interiors from step 1.1 imply the same shrinking for the discs $hB_i$. These discs are locally finite off $\Lambda_{G_i}$. Otherwise choose distinct cosets with discs meeting every neighborhood of some $x\notin\Lambda_{G_i}$. Their diameters shrink, so the images of every one of three fixed distinct points of $S$ tend to $x$. Step 1.2 applied to their matrices leaves at most one exceptional source point, and forces $x\in\Lambda_{G_i}$, a contradiction. In particular, at $x\in S^\circ$ no disc $hB_i$, $h\notin J$, contains or accumulates at $x$: containment is excluded by precise invariance and accumulation by local finiteness. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, construct, algebra]

Fix $x\in S^\circ$. It is regular for both factors by the given intersection equality. Choose a small open neighborhood $W$ of $x$ disjoint from every $hB_i$ with $h\in G_i\setminus J$, for both $i$, using step 2.1. Shrink it so that $hW\cap W=\varnothing$ for every nonidentity $h$ in either factor, using properness at $x$ in [F3]. For $h\in G_i\setminus J$, disjointness of $W$ from $h^{-1}B_i$ gives $hW\subset U_{3-i}$. Applying an alternating reduced word of length at least two to $W$, its last-applied letter $h\in G_i\setminus J$ therefore leaves the whole image in $hU_i\subset hB_i$, which is disjoint from $W$. Words of length one and elements of $J$ were already excluded. Thus $gW\cap W=\varnothing$ for every $g\ne1$ in $G$, so $x\in\Omega(G)$. Conversely $\Lambda_J\subset\Lambda_G$. We have proved $S\cap\Omega(G)=S^\circ$. The same word argument, beginning at a point of $S^\circ$ rather than its neighborhood, shows that no reduced word outside $J$ sends it to another point of $S^\circ$: a length-one such letter sends it strictly into the opposite open disc, and subsequent letters keep it in an outermost translated disc disjoint from $S^\circ$. Hence $S^\circ$ is precisely invariant under $J$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

Now apply [F2] with ambient group $G$ and compact invariant set $S$. Step 3.1 supplies exactly $S\cap\Lambda_G=\Lambda_J$; the rank-one clearance of $S$ is unchanged. Therefore the circles $gS$ shrink over distinct right cosets $gJ$. No finite-generation or geometric-finiteness property of $G$ is used in this application. [F2, step 3.1, given, algebra]

The actual coset graph has vertices $G/G_1$ and $G/G_2$, edges $G/J$, with $gJ$ joining $gG_1$ to $gG_2$. It is connected by writing a finite factor word. It is a tree: removing immediate reversals from a closed edge path would give a nonempty alternating word outside $J$ equal to an element of $J$, contradicting [F1] after absorbing that last element. Its edge $gJ$ carries the circle $gS$; the half-space pointing from $gG_i$ towards $gG_{3-i}$ is $gB_i$. At a vertex $gG_i$, the outgoing discs are $ghB_i$, $hJ\in G_i/J$. Their interiors are disjoint, their boundary intersections are in $g\Lambda_{G_i}$, and their complement within $g\Omega(G_i)$ is $gR_i$. Along a nonbacktracking path these forward closed discs are nested. For two successive edges this is $hB_i\subset B_{3-i}$ from step 1.1 after changing coordinates by the initial prefix; induction proves the assertion along the path. This also shows that translated circles do not cross: connect their edges by the unique finite path and use its nested half-spaces. If two translated circles meet at a regular point for $G$, translate one to $S^\circ$ and use its precise invariance from step 3.1; the cosets must agree. Thus every contact of distinct circles lies in $\Lambda_G$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

A point of $R_i$ on one of the outgoing circles $hS$ is regular for $G$ by step 3.1, since it is regular for $G_i$ and hence not in $h\Lambda_J$. A point of $R_i$ on none of those circles has a neighborhood $W$ disjoint from all $hB_i$, by step 2.1, and with disjoint nonidentity $G_i$ translates. Any reduced word outside $G_i$ is written with a possible left prefix in $G_i$, followed by a letter in $G_{3-i}\setminus J$, and a possible right suffix in $G_i$. The right suffix preserves $R_i$ and its neighborhood's disjointness from the outgoing discs. The first letter outside $G_i$ sends that neighborhood into $U_i$; further alternating letters and the left prefix put it in an outgoing $G_i$ disc, disjoint from $W$. To make the neighborhood assertion uniform over the suffix, take $\mathcal W=G_iW$: it is disjoint from all $hB_i$, is contained in $U_{3-i}$, and its image under every letter of $G_{3-i}\setminus J$ is contained in $U_i$. The same reduced-word induction applies to $\mathcal W$. Thus no word outside $G_i$ maps $W$ back into itself. This proves $R_i\subset\Omega(G)$ in all cases. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.2, construct, algebra]

Take a point $x$ outside $G(R_1\cup R_2)$ and outside $G(\Lambda_{G_1}\cup\Lambda_{G_2})$. If it lies on an edge circle, it lies in that edge's regular seam and hence in both adjacent retained regions, a contradiction. At an initial vertex it therefore belongs to the interior of exactly one outgoing disc: otherwise it is in that vertex's retained region. Move across that edge and repeat. The reverse edge is not chosen, since its forward disc is the complementary half-space and $x$ is in the previous forward disc's interior. This constructs an infinite nonbacktracking path. Its edges are distinct cosets, its forward discs are nested, and step 4.1 makes their boundaries shrink. Step 1.2 makes their discs shrink, so their intersection is exactly $\{x\}$. Write their edge representatives $g_n$. The images of three fixed distinct points of $S$ tend to $x$; the rank-one matrix argument of step 1.2 implies $x\in\Lambda_G$. Conversely if a point is enclosed by such an infinite path, the same argument proves it is in $\Lambda_G$. Together with step 5.1 this proves both the asserted nested-disc characterization outside the factor limit sets and $\Omega(G)=G(R_1\cup R_2)$. [F3, step 1.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

It remains to check the quotient including its topology. In the tree description a regular point belongs to at most two vertex retained regions. If two vertices are separated by two or more edges, the path's first two half-spaces force a point common to their regions onto their edge-circle contact; step 4.2 excludes such contacts in $\Omega(G)$. The regions of two adjacent vertices meet exactly in that edge's regular seam, and its stabilizer is precisely the conjugate of $J$ by step 3.1. Every nonempty retained region contains an interior point: this is immediate off its outgoing circles, and follows from the two-sided neighborhood in step 3.1 at a regular seam. For a nonempty vertex retained region its stabilizer is its factor group: a word leaving that vertex puts any nonseam regular point in an outgoing disc as in step 5.1; a seam point can return to that same vertex only through its factor's existing seam translates. Thus all orbit identifications between $R_1$ and $R_2$ are exactly the stated factor identifications and the common seam identification. Locally away from seams, step 5.1 gives an ordinary factor-quotient chart. At a seam point, the neighborhood $W$ from step 3.1 has disjoint nonidentity $G$ translates; its two closed sides $W\cap B_1,W\cap B_2$ are precisely the two incident retained pieces, because $W$ avoids every other outgoing disc. Gluing these sides by the identity recovers $W$ with its original topology and conformal sphere chart. These local descriptions prove that the induced bijection from the stated glued quotient to $\Omega(G)/G$ is a homeomorphism, and has the specified conformal structure. They also cover empty seams and disconnected regions. No conical classification of the new nested points, cusp-rank computation or geometrical-finiteness conclusion has entered the proof. [F3, step 3.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

and scope

The actual published Space I paper was read through PDF pp. 2–39, printed pp. 1097–1134, including all main combination proofs. The author reread the actual printed pp. 1114–1121 while developing this local block/tree proof. Its PDF SHA256 is 9a90e6bb93ea5d579c5a2cb62fdb2341539e4542a3ae4d9f03ee63c962b0b873. The earlier arXiv theorem has different geometric-finiteness hypotheses and is not substituted for the published theorem. Actual complete algebraic-amalgam and null-coset supplier proofs were read. The proof does not assume the resulting group is geometrically finite in order to obtain its shrinking edge-circle family: regularity at the original seam is proved first.

The full geometric-finiteness combination theorem additionally needs the conical behavior of the new nested points and the strong-block cusp compatibility, particularly when new parabolics or parabolic rank enlargement occur. Those operations, and the original generic hyperbolization theorem, remain separate obligations.

inventory.full_statement:
Assume AC and all the hypotheses of [[thm-blocked-jordan-amalgams-have-the-prescribed-conformal-boundary-gluing]], with its notation $G,G_i,J,S$. Impose the following seam-parabolic compatibility: if $p$ is a parabolic point of $J$ and its full stabilizer in $G$ has rank one, then in the coordinate making that stabilizer a real translation lattice there is $R_p<\infty$ such that
$$\Lambda_G\setminus\{p\}\subset\{|\operatorname{Im}z|\le R_p\}.$$
No additional condition is imposed if the full ambient stabilizer has rank two. In particular rank-one subgroup cusps may enlarge to rank two. Then every point of
$$\Lambda_G\setminus G(\Lambda_{G_1}\cup\Lambda_{G_2})$$
is a conical limit point of $G$.

The subgroup $J$ may be trivial, cyclic loxodromic, cyclic parabolic, rank-two parabolic, or nonelementary geometrically finite. The factor groups need not be geometrically finite. Compatibility is an explicit additional interface to be proved in an application; geometric finiteness of $G$ is not assumed or asserted here.

actual_proof_anchors.quote: Fix a new limit point $x$. From [F1] take nested forward discs enclosing $x$. By passing to a subsequence of edge types write them $h_nB$, with one fixed $B\in\{B_1,B_2\}$ and $h_nS$ their boundaries. The discs shrink to $x$ and omit each fixed point $y\ne x$ eventually. Put $y_n=h_n^{-1}x$. None belongs to $\Lambda_J$, since otherwise $x$ belongs to a translated factor limit set. They belong to $\Lambda_G$, by invariance. We shall construct $j_n\in J$ and either no further normalization or a parabolic translation $q_n\in G$ such that the spherical distance from $q_nj_ny_n$ to every point of $q_nS$ is at least a fixed $\delta>0$. Fixed coordinate changes in finitely many cusp frames do not affect this assertion, since their sphere maps and inverses are uniformly continuous. [A1, F1, given, construct, algebra]

We justify ideal Dirichlet representatives when $J$ is nonelementary. In the ball model centered at a chosen Dirichlet center $o\in C(\Lambda_J)$, a regular point $y\in\Omega(J)$ has a representative in the ideal boundary of $D_J(o)$. To see this, the spherical conformal scale of $j$ at $y$ tends to zero as $j$ escapes $J$: normalize its matrices to rank one as in [F1]'s proof. Its kernel point belongs to $\Lambda_J$ by applying the same normalization to the inverse matrices and evaluating at an interior point. Since $y$ is outside that closed limit set, the matrix denominator is bounded away from zero on a small neighborhood of $y$, while the normalized determinant tends to zero. The fractional-linear derivative formula therefore gives scale tending to zero. Thus the scale attains its positive maximum at some $j$. At $z=jy$, every $a\in J$ has scale at most one, by the derivative chain rule and maximality. The ideal Dirichlet inequality $d(w,o)\le d(w,a^{-1}o)$ on a ray $w\to z$ is exactly the boundary scale inequality $|a'(z)|_{\rm sph}\le1$: take the limit of the hyperbolic distance difference using the ball distance formula, or equivalently its Poisson factor $(1-|a^{-1}o|^2)/|z-a^{-1}o|^2$. Hence $z\in\overline D_J(o)$. This proves the needed representative assertion instead of assuming coverage of the ideal boundary from model-domain coverage alone. [F1, F5, construct, algebra]

Suppose first that $J$ is nonelementary. Choose $j_n$ as in step 1.2 and put $z_n=j_ny_n\in\overline D_J(o)$. These points still lie in $\Lambda_G\setminus\Lambda_J$. If their distances from $S$ have a positive lower bound along a subsequence, take $q_n=1$ there and obtain the target separation. Otherwise pass to a subsequence $z_n\to p\in S$. Closedness of $\Lambda_G$ and [F1] give $p\in\Lambda_J$, and [F2] makes $p$ one of finitely many parabolic vertices of the Dirichlet domain. At a rank-two $J$ cusp the two parallel-coordinate bounds on ideal points of $D_J$ prevent $z_n\to\infty$ in that cusp frame, since these are finite ideal points. Therefore $J_p$ has rank one. Normalize its generator as $z\mapsto z+\ell$, $\ell>0$. Its Dirichlet inequalities bound $\operatorname{Re}z_n$, while $z_n\to\infty$ forces $|\operatorname{Im}z_n|\to\infty$. If $G_p$ has rank one, the given compatibility bounds $\operatorname{Im}z_n$ on $\Lambda_G$, a contradiction. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, construct, algebra]

The remaining case is rank-one $J_p$ and rank-two $G_p$. In the same cusp coordinate, $S\setminus\{p\}$ has $|\operatorname{Im}z|\le R_S$ by the original clearance. Choose a second lattice vector $v$ of $G_p$ with $\operatorname{Im}v\ne0$. Real multiples of $\ell$ and integer multiples of $v$ reduce every $z_n$ into a fixed bounded parallelogram; explicitly first reduce the imaginary coordinate modulo $\operatorname{Im}v$, then its real coordinate modulo $\ell$. Let $q_n$ be the corresponding ambient translation. Its imaginary part tends in absolute value to infinity, with the opposite sign to $\operatorname{Im}z_n$. Thus $q_nz_n$ stays in a fixed finite compact set, whereas every finite point of $q_nS$ has imaginary part tending uniformly to infinity in absolute value; its possible point infinity is unchanged. Consequently $q_nS\to\{p\}$ uniformly in spherical diameter, with every point tending to $p$, and its distance from $q_nz_n$ has a fixed positive lower bound. This proves the required separation in this case as well. Since the preceding alternatives cover every subsequence that fails the unmodified separation, they suffice in constructing a conical subsequence. No bound on a new rank-two cusp's transverse limit set was required. [F3, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

For completeness handle every elementary $J$ directly. If $J$ is trivial, take $j_n=q_n=1$: compactness and $S\cap\Lambda_G=\varnothing$ separate all $y_n\in\Lambda_G$ from $S$. If $J$ is loxodromic cyclic, put its fixed points at $0,\infty$ and its generator in the form $z\mapsto az$, $|a|>1$. Integer powers put each $z_n=j_ny_n$ in $1\le|z|\le|a|$. That compact annulus avoids $\Lambda_J$; a limit of its points in $\Lambda_G$ cannot belong to $S$ by [F1]. Hence there is again uniform separation with $q_n=1$. If $J$ is rank-two parabolic, translations put $z_n$ in a fixed finite closed parallelogram, away from its only limit point infinity, giving the same argument. If $J$ is rank-one parabolic, real translations put $\operatorname{Re}z_n$ in a bounded interval. A bounded-imaginary subsequence lies in a finite compact set and is separated from $S$. If imaginary parts are unbounded, the ambient rank-one compatibility rules this out when $G_p$ has rank one, while rank two is handled exactly by step 3.1. These are all elementary possibilities: torsion-free discreteness excludes elliptics, a preserved limit pair admits no interchange of order two and hence gives a diagonal cyclic group, and a unique limit point gives a translation lattice. A finite limit set of size at least three makes the group finite by its faithful permutation action, hence trivial. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

On the subsequence supplied by steps 2.1–4.1 set $k_n=q_nj_nh_n^{-1}\in G$. The circle $k_n(h_nS)=q_nS$ has distance at least $\delta$ from $k_nx$. Because $h_nS$ separates $x$ from every fixed $y\ne x$ for sufficiently large $n$, $q_nS$ separates $k_nx$ from $k_ny$. The spherical ball of radius $\delta$ about $k_nx$ misses $q_nS$ and lies in its one complementary component. Therefore $d_{\rm sph}(k_nx,k_ny)\ge\delta$ for every fixed $y\ne x$ and all sufficiently large $n$. This uses separation by a Jordan circle, not the stronger unsupported claim that a sphere distance increases to every transformed boundary point. The matrices $k_n$ escape compact sets: otherwise a compact subsequence and its sphere equicontinuity would send $h_nS\to\{x\}$ to circles approaching $k_nx$, contradicting the same lower distance bound. Normalize their matrices and take a rank-one subsequence. Its kernel point must be $x$: if it were another point, $k_nx$ and $k_ny$ for a fixed point avoiding both it and $x$ would have the same image limit, contrary to their separation. Thus every boundary point other than $x$ has one common image limit, whereas a further subsequence of $k_nx$ has a limit at distance at least $\delta$ from it. Criterion [F4] proves $x$ conical. Every possible elementary and nonelementary normalization case was covered, completing the assertion. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

inventory.actual_source_notes:
and remaining interface

The complete actual published Space I combination proof was read, including printed pp. 1127–1128; its PDF SHA256 is 9a90e6bb93ea5d579c5a2cb62fdb2341539e4542a3ae4d9f03ee63c962b0b873. The complete actual structural, standard-cusp, local-classifier and intrinsic-conical suppliers were read. The source's stronger comparison of distances to arbitrary transformed points is not needed: the valid conclusion follows from separation by the transformed Jordan circle and a uniform ball around the image of $x$.

The remaining application obligation is genuine: the rank-one ambient boundedness at seam parabolics must be established from the particular finite peripheral gluing data. It is not a consequence of a mere algebraic amalgam assertion, and is not assumed covertly as geometric finiteness. This theorem by itself neither proves the full geometric-finiteness combination theorem nor resolves original generic hyperbolization.

inventory.full_statement:
Assume AC and all the blocked Jordan amalgam hypotheses and the explicit seam-parabolic compatibility of [[thm-bounded-seam-parabolics-make-new-amalgam-limit-points-conical]]. Assume in addition that each factor $G_i$ is elementary or nonelementary geometrically finite. Then $G=\langle G_1,G_2\rangle$ is nonelementary geometrically finite: every positive-radius neighborhood of its convex hull has finite quotient volume.

Every parabolic point of $G$ is a translate of a parabolic point of one of the factors and is bounded parabolic. At a factor parabolic point outside all translates in that factor of the gluing circle, a rank-one factor stabilizer remains the full ambient stabilizer and has a precisely invariant ideal peak contained in the retained conformal piece. At seam parabolics rank enlargement from one to two is allowed, subject to the stated compatibility when the final rank remains one. No closed-disc disjointness, absence of new parabolic elements, finite-sided polyhedron or unproved general geometrical-finiteness combination theorem is assumed.

Compatibility remains an actual application hypothesis; this theorem does not establish it for a given peripheral gluing.

actual_proof_anchors.quote: Choose $a\in G_1\setminus J$ and $b\in G_2\setminus J$. Their commutator is an alternating reduced word of length four, hence is nonidentity by [F2]. Thus $G$ is nonabelian and therefore nonelementary by [F4]. A parabolic fixed point of any such $G$ cannot be conical. Normalize it to infinity. By [F5] its model orbit has height bounded above by a fixed $H$. A ray towards infinity has height tending to infinity, and the distance from its point of height $Y$ to every orbit point is at least $\log(Y/H)$, from the upper half-space metric. This diverges, excluding conicality. Conicality for a subgroup passes to the ambient group simply by using the same orbit sequence and ray. Every nonparabolic factor limit point is conical, either by [F3] or directly on the axis for an elementary loxodromic group. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, construct, algebra]

Let $p$ be a factor parabolic point. If it belongs to a factor translate $hS$, the block equality gives $h^{-1}p\in\Lambda_J$. That point cannot be conical for $J$, because it is parabolic in $G$ by step 1.1; for nonelementary geometrically finite $J$ it is therefore parabolic in $J$, and the elementary cases give the same conclusion. Its ambient stabilizer is a translation lattice. If its rank is one, the explicit compatibility bounds the transverse coordinate of $\Lambda_G$; its quotient by the real translation is then a closed subset of a compact cylinder and is compact. If its rank is two, $(\Lambda_G\setminus\{p\})/G_p$ is a closed subset of the compact plane lattice quotient and is again compact. Thus every seam parabolic is bounded, with rank enlargement allowed. [F3, F4, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

Suppose now $p\in\Lambda_{G_i}$ is parabolic but lies on no $G_i$ translate of $S$. If its factor stabilizer has rank two, its ambient stabilizer also has rank two and boundedness follows as in step 2.1. Consider rank one, normalizing $p=\infty$ and $H=(G_i)_p$ as real translations of period $\ell$. There is a precisely invariant factor peak $P=\{|\operatorname{Im}z|>R\}\subset\Omega(G_i)$, by [F3]; for an elementary rank-one parabolic factor it is immediate from its translation action and its unique limit point. The compact disc $B_i$ excludes $p$, since $B_i\cap\Lambda_{G_i}=\Lambda_J\subset S$ and $p\notin S$. It therefore has bounded finite coordinates in this normalization. The $H$ translates of $B_i$ have a uniform transverse bound. We claim that all $G_i$ translates have one uniform transverse bound as well. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

Otherwise choose $g_n\in G_i$ with some point of $g_nB_i$ having imaginary part unbounded in absolute value. They cannot eventually belong to $H$. Fix $y_0\in P$. For $g_n\notin H$, precise invariance of $P$ implies $g_ny_0\notin P$, so these imaginary coordinates are bounded by $R$. Left-multiply by $t_n\in H$ to put their real coordinates in $[0,\ell]$. Then $t_ng_ny_0$ remains in a fixed finite compact rectangle, while the discs $t_ng_nB_i$ still have unbounded transverse extent. Their right cosets modulo $J$ cannot belong to a finite set, because each fixed translate of $B_i$ excludes infinity: $p$ lies on no factor translate of $S$ and no factor translate of $\Lambda_J$, so it cannot belong to any factor translate of $B_i$ by the block equality. Each such fixed disc is compact in the finite plane and has bounded transverse coordinate. Pass to distinct cosets. The shrinking-disc assertion in [F2], together with a point in each disc escaping to infinity, forces every point of each disc to approach infinity spherically. In particular the images of three fixed distinct points in $B_i$ approach infinity. Matrix convergence in [F5] then has attracting point infinity and exceptional point in $\Lambda_{G_i}$. Since $y_0\in\Omega(G_i)$, it is not exceptional, so $t_ng_ny_0\to\infty$, contradicting its fixed finite rectangle. This proves the claim. [F2, F5, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Enlarge $R$ to $R'$ exceeding that uniform bound and its original value. The smaller peak $P'=\{|\operatorname{Im}z|>R'\}$ is contained in $\Omega(G_i)$ and avoids every outgoing closed disc, hence lies in the retained region $R_i$. By [F2], $gP'\cap P'=\varnothing$ for $g\notin G_i$; within $G_i$ its precise invariance under $H$ follows from $P'\subset P$ and the translation invariance of both. Any ambient element fixing infinity is a translation by [F4], and its image of the two-tail region $P'$ necessarily intersects $P'$ (already sufficiently large positive imaginary parts lie in both). Thus no such element lies outside $G_i$, and the full ambient stabilizer is exactly $H$. Also $P'\subset\Omega(G)$ by [F2], so $\Lambda_G\setminus\{p\}$ has bounded transverse coordinate. Its quotient by $H$ is closed in a compact cylinder, proving $p$ bounded parabolic and the asserted precisely invariant peak and stabilizer conclusions. [F2, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Every ambient parabolic point belongs to a translated factor limit set: otherwise [F1] makes it conical, contradicted by step 1.1. Translate it into a factor limit set. If it were not parabolic for that factor, its conicality from step 1.1 would again contradict ambient parabolicity. Hence it is a factor parabolic point and steps 2.1–5.1 show it bounded. Finally every ambient limit point in a translated factor limit set is either a conical factor point or a now-bounded factor parabolic point. Every remaining limit point is conical by [F1]. Thus every point of $\Lambda_G$ is conical or bounded parabolic.
